scenes.tts: The T cell receptor reads a short peptide held in the groove of an M H C protein. Blocking a brake helps only if the patient already has T cells that recognise the tumour. The other approach gives T cells a new receptor. Can you build one from parts?
scenes.caption: The T cell receptor reads a short peptide held in the groove of an MHC protein. Blocking a brake helps only if the patient already has T cells that recognise the tumour. The other approach gives T cells a new receptor. Can you build one from parts?
scenes.visual: A T cell receptor reads a peptide on an MHC protein; a note says the brake approach needs T cells that already recognise the tumour; the receptor is replaced by a dashed question-mark box, a new receptor built from parts.
scenes.narration: The T cell receptor reads a short peptide held in the groove of an MHC protein. Blocking a brake helps only if the patient already has T cells that recognise the tumour. The other approach gives T cells a new receptor. Can you build one from parts?

scenes.tts: In 1989, Gideon Gross, Tova Waks and Zelig Eshhar joined the variable regions of an antibody to the constant regions of T cell receptor chains. T cells carrying the hybrid responded to the antibody's target. Yoshihisa Kuwana and colleagues had published the same kind of construct in 1987.
scenes.caption: In 1989, Gideon Gross, Tova Waks and Zelig Eshhar joined the variable regions of an antibody to the constant regions of T cell receptor chains. T cells carrying the hybrid responded to the antibody's target. Yoshihisa Kuwana and colleagues had published the same kind of construct in 1987.
scenes.visual: The receptor's own tips drop away; two antibody variable regions join the constant regions of the receptor chains. The hybrid reaches a target on a cell and the T cell responds. A credit to Kuwana and colleagues, 1987, appears last.
scenes.narration: In 1989, Gideon Gross, Tova Waks and Zelig Eshhar joined the variable regions of an antibody to the constant regions of T cell receptor chains. T cells carrying the hybrid responded to the antibody's target. Yoshihisa Kuwana and colleagues had published the same kind of construct in 1987.

scenes.tts: The receptor's own tips read a peptide held on an M H C protein. An antibody is different. It grips a whole folded protein directly. So such a receptor needs no peptide and no M H C protein.
scenes.caption: The receptor's own tips read a peptide held on an MHC protein. An antibody is different. It grips a whole folded protein directly. So such a receptor needs no peptide and no MHC protein.
scenes.visual: Two panels: the receptor's own tips read a peptide on MHC; an antibody-tipped receptor grips a whole folded protein directly, with crossed-out peptide and MHC chips beside it.
scenes.narration: The receptor's own tips read a peptide held on an MHC protein. An antibody is different. It grips a whole folded protein directly. So such a receptor needs no peptide and no MHC protein.

scenes.tts: Later designs, from Eshhar's laboratory and others, were single chains. They put an antibody fragment outside the cell and the zeta tail inside. This is a chimeric antigen receptor, or C A R. Remember the plan: antibody outside, zeta tail inside.
scenes.caption: Later designs, from Eshhar's laboratory and others, were single chains. They put an antibody fragment outside the cell and the zeta tail inside. This is a chimeric antigen receptor, or CAR. Remember the plan: antibody outside, zeta tail inside.
scenes.visual: The two-chain hybrid becomes one chain: an antibody fragment outside the membrane, the zeta tail inside. The name CAR appears; the fragment and tail are highlighted last.
